content:
The Fried frailty phenotype is a way of describing frailty using five physical signs. It was developed by Linda Fried and colleagues in 2001 and is widely used in research and some clinics. If you have painful joints, arthritis can affect several of the five signs, so it helps to know what they are and how to explain your situation.

This guide explains the five criteria, how they relate to arthritis, how the phenotype differs from the Clinical Frailty Scale, and what you can do. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

The five criteria

  • Unintentional weight loss, for example losing a noticeable amount of weight in the past year without trying.
  • Exhaustion, feeling that everything is an effort much of the time.
  • Weak grip strength, usually measured with a hand-held device.
  • Slow walking speed, timed over a short distance.
  • Low physical activity.

In the original research, people with three or more signs were described as frail, one or two as prefrail, and none as robust.

How arthritis can affect the criteria

Hand arthritis can lower grip strength. Hip, knee or foot arthritis can slow walking. Pain and inflammation can cause tiredness and make people less active. This means arthritis can make you score as more frail than you are overall, or it can be a real driver of frailty because pain leads to less movement. Tell clinicians which signs you think are due to your joints and which feel new.

How it differs from the Clinical Frailty Scale

The Clinical Frailty Scale, developed by Kenneth Rockwood and colleagues, is a 9-point scale based on a clinician's judgement of how fit you are and how much help you need day to day. It is quick and often used in hospitals. The Fried phenotype uses measured physical signs instead. Neither is a diagnosis on its own, and both are snapshots that can change.

What you can do

Frailty and prefrailty can sometimes improve. Things that may help include:

  • Strength and balance exercise, ideally guided by a physiotherapist or class.
  • Eating enough, including protein at each meal; tell your GP about weight loss.
  • A medicines review, especially if you take several medicines.
  • Treating arthritis pain well, so you can stay active.
  • Checking eyesight, hearing and feet.

Talking to your clinician

  • Ask which frailty measure was used and what your result means.
  • Explain how arthritis affects your grip, walking and energy.
  • Ask what can be done to improve things, and when it will be reviewed.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for unplanned weight loss, ongoing exhaustion or a steady decline over weeks.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can I measure this myself?

Some parts, such as weight and activity, are easy to notice yourself, but grip and walking speed are usually measured by clinicians. Tell your GP if you notice changes.

Does a frailty label mean I cannot have treatment?

No. It helps clinicians plan safer care. Ask how it affects decisions about your treatment.

Can frailty improve if my arthritis does not?

Sometimes. Exercise, nutrition, a medicines review and better pain control can all help.
